x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB sends traffic from the private subnets to DynamoDB over the AWS network, with no internet path. It is the most secure option and has no extra charge.
x.B: A NAT gateway sends traffic through an internet gateway to the public DynamoDB endpoint, so the traffic leaves the AWS network path and costs extra.
x.C: A NAT instance has the same internet path problem and needs management.
x.D: An internet gateway sends traffic over the internet and requires public IPs, which isn't possible for instances in private subnets.

x.A: ElastiCache for Redis would need code changes to read from and populate the cache, so the application would be reconfigured.
x.B: DAX is an in-memory cache built for DynamoDB that is compatible with the DynamoDB API, so read-heavy tables get microsecond reads with almost no application change, and it is fully managed.
x.C: Global tables replicate data to other Regions for availability and locality. They don't speed up reads in one Region.
x.D: ElastiCache for Memcached also needs application changes for caching logic, plus cluster management.

x.A: AWS Backup centrally manages backups for EC2 and RDS and can copy them to another Region on a schedule, so it needs the least effort.
x.B: Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshots and AMIs. It doesn't manage RDS backups.
x.C: Creating AMIs, copying them, and managing a read replica separately are manual steps that need to be repeated and maintained.
x.D: Snapshots, exports to S3, and replication are several separate manual steps to maintain, which is a lot of overhead.

x.A: An IAM role attached to the EC2 instance, with read access to the parameter and Decrypt permission on the KMS key, lets the application securely retrieve the secure parameter with temporary credentials.
x.B: A policy can't be assigned to an EC2 instance directly. It has to be attached to a role.
x.C: A trust relationship between a parameter and an instance doesn't exist, and RDS isn't the principal that reads the parameter.
x.D: A trust relationship between the DB instance and EC2 doesn't give the application access to Parameter Store.

x.A: AWS WAF can't be associated with a Network Load Balancer, because it works at layer 7 with ALB, API Gateway, and CloudFront.
x.B: Shield Advanced protects the NLB with enhanced detection and mitigation of large, sophisticated DDoS attacks, and includes access to the response team.
x.C: AWS WAF can be associated with API Gateway to block web exploits such as SQL injection.
x.D: GuardDuty only detects threats and doesn't mitigate attacks, and Shield Standard gives basic protection only.
x.E: Shield Standard is already on by default, and it gives only basic protection, not protection against large, sophisticated DDoS attacks.

x.A: An SQS queue decouples the producers and consumers of the microservices. The queue buffers work, consumers can scale independently, and since order doesn't matter, a standard queue is fine.
x.B: SNS pushes to subscribers and doesn't hold messages for consumers to process at their own rate, so work can be lost if a consumer is busy.
x.C: A Lambda function to pass messages adds a custom component and doesn't buffer or retry messages.
x.D: DynamoDB Streams isn't designed as a messaging layer between microservices, and it needs more code.

x.A: RDS doesn't offer a deployment with synchronous replication to three nodes in three AZs for MySQL in this way. Multi-AZ uses two.
x.B: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ synchronously replicates each transaction to a standby in another AZ, so every transaction is on at least two nodes, and it fails over automatically.
x.C: Cross-Region read replicas replicate asynchronously, not synchronously, so some data could be lost.
x.D: A self-managed MySQL on EC2 triggering Lambda is custom, not synchronous in a reliable way, and has high operational overhead.

x.A: S3 and CloudFront serve static content, API Gateway and Lambda serve dynamic content, and DynamoDB on-demand scales read and write capacity almost instantly. There are no servers to patch.
x.B: Aurora Auto Scaling scales read replicas, but not writes, and takes longer to react than DynamoDB on-demand.
x.C: EC2 instances need patching and maintenance, and provisioned write capacity doesn't scale as quickly as on-demand.
x.D: EC2 instances need patching, and Aurora writes don't scale with Auto Scaling, so it doesn't meet the requirements.

x.A: Configuring the Lambda function to run in the VPC attaches network interfaces in the VPC, so the function can use the existing Direct Connect path to reach the on-premises database. The security group controls access.
x.B: A new VPN is unnecessary because Direct Connect already connects the VPC to the data center.
x.C: Route tables in the VPC don't apply to a Lambda function unless the function is configured to run in the VPC.
x.D: A Lambda function can't send traffic through an Elastic IP without a network interface, and EIPs are not attached to functions.

x.A: There's no way to allow access from ECS by updating an S3 role like this, and relaunching a container doesn't grant permissions.
x.B: A task role is an IAM role that gives the containers in a task the permissions to call AWS APIs. Specifying it as taskRoleArn in the task definition lets the application access S3.
x.C: Security groups control network traffic and don't grant permissions to call the S3 API.
x.D: Using an IAM user's credentials by relaunching instances isn't how ECS provides credentials, and long-lived keys are insecure.

x.A: A volume gateway presents iSCSI block volumes, and they can't be shared by multiple instances as a Windows file system.
x.B: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed SMB file shares that multiple Windows instances across AZs can mount at the same time, with Multi-AZ availability.
x.C: EFS uses the NFS protocol and isn't supported on Windows instances.
x.D: A standard EBS volume attaches to one instance in one AZ, so it can't be shared across multiple instances in different AZs.

x.A: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically, so the database is highly available with no manual intervention.
x.B: A DB instance with replicas in another AZ doesn't fail over automatically in standard RDS, so it needs manual promotion.
x.C: A self-managed Docker cluster on EC2 means managing the hosts and cluster, which is more manual work.
x.D: ECS with Fargate runs containers without managing servers and scales automatically, with little manual intervention.
x.E: ECS with the EC2 launch type still needs the EC2 hosts to be provisioned, patched, and scaled, which is more manual work.

x.A: AWS Transfer Family offers a fully managed, highly available SFTP endpoint that writes directly to S3, so there are no servers to manage.
x.B: S3 File Gateway provides NFS and SMB access, not SFTP, so partners can't use it as an SFTP server.
x.C: A single EC2 instance isn't highly available, and the VPN and cron job add operational work.
x.D: Running SFTP servers on EC2 behind an NLB is available, but you have to manage the servers, patching, and scripts, which is a lot of overhead.

x.A: Governance mode lets users with special permissions override the lock, so documents could be deleted during the 5 years.
x.B: Compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from overwriting or deleting the documents for the retention period, which meets the requirement.
x.C: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 and you can't configure rotation yourself.
x.D: KMS customer managed keys support automatic yearly rotation, which meets the key rotation requirement with little work.
x.E: Imported key material can't be rotated automatically, so it adds manual work each year.

x.A: S3 static hosting with Lambda doesn't suit an existing Java and PHP application and would need a rewrite.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk is a managed platform for Java and PHP applications with high availability. Swapping environment URLs lets you test new features and switch over easily, with minimal operational overhead.
x.C: EC2 with Auto Scaling and an ALB works but you manage the servers and platforms yourself, so it has more overhead.
x.D: Containerizing and using the Load Balancer Controller needs a Kubernetes setup and more effort, so it isn't minimal overhead.

x.A: A read replica lets employees run reporting queries without loading the primary instance, so order processing no longer times out, and reports still work.
x.B: Sending the ordering application's writes to a read replica isn't possible, because replicas are read-only.
x.C: Migrating to DynamoDB would need a major redesign of the application and doesn't fit reporting queries with SQL.
x.D: Scheduling reports for non-peak hours stops employees from running queries during business hours, which isn't allowed.

x.A: A MySQL database on EC2 means managing a server and doesn't scale as well as a managed or serverless option.
x.B: Writing the extracted data to S3 and using Athena lets an application run SQL queries on it without servers, which scales well.
x.C: A custom application on an Auto Scaling group means building and maintaining text extraction code, which is a lot of overhead.
x.D: Rekognition isn't meant for converting scanned documents to text, and Transcribe Medical works on audio, not text.
x.E: Textract converts scanned documents to text, and Comprehend Medical extracts medical information from the text. Lambda runs the workflow when new documents are uploaded.

x.A: Read replicas offload reads, but you would have to manage and point the application at multiple replicas for multiple databases, and they don't reduce reads as much as a cache.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis caches frequent reads in memory, reducing database reads, and it supports replication and Multi-AZ failover for high availability.
x.C: DNS caching in Route 53 doesn't cache database query results.
x.D: ElastiCache for Memcached caches reads but has no replication or built-in failover, so it doesn't provide high availability.

x.A: Two instances in different AZs configured as a cluster with replication give automatic failover if a disruptive event occurs, so the database is highly available.
x.B: Restoring from an AMI with CloudFormation is a slow, manual-style recovery with downtime and data loss, so it isn't automatic failover.
x.C: A cross-Region setup is more complex than needed, and the question asks for high availability and automatic failover within normal operation.
x.D: EC2 automatic recovery restarts the same instance on new hardware. It doesn't provide failover to a second database node and has downtime.

x.A: An EventBridge rule targeting an ECS task doesn't hold the orders durably, so orders may still be lost if a processor fails.
x.B: An ALB sends requests directly to instances, and if the instance fails during processing, the order is lost and has to be resent.
x.C: Putting orders in an SQS queue stores them durably, and the Auto Scaling group's instances consume messages. If an instance fails, the message becomes visible again and another instance processes it, so no manual reprocessing is needed.
x.D: SNS with Lambda and Run Command is a convoluted design, and SNS doesn't hold messages if a consumer fails.

x.A: Redeploying the stack every 30 days would lose data and cause disruption, and isn't a data expiry solution.
x.B: A Marketplace monitoring tool and a delete script on EC2 add cost and development work.
x.C: A Lambda function invoked on new items to delete old ones means writing code and paying for the invocations and delete operations.
x.D: DynamoDB TTL deletes items automatically after the timestamp in a TTL attribute passes, at no extra cost, with minimal development.

x.A: Refactoring to Lambda functions on .NET Core is a big change and goes against minimizing development changes.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk's .NET platform on Windows runs the application with minimal code changes, and a Multi-AZ deployment gives high availability.
x.C: Running on Amazon Linux means changing the Windows .NET application, which could need code changes.
x.D: Migrating from Oracle to DynamoDB changes the data model entirely, requiring large code changes.
x.E: DMS to Oracle on RDS Multi-AZ keeps the same database engine so the application's code doesn't change, and Multi-AZ provides high availability.

x.A: ECS with MongoDB on EC2 means changing the deployment method from Kubernetes and managing the database yourself.
x.B: ECS and DynamoDB change both the orchestration and the database API, which requires code and deployment changes.
x.C: EKS keeps Kubernetes, but DynamoDB doesn't use the MongoDB API, so the code would need changes.
x.D: EKS keeps the Kubernetes deployment method, Fargate removes node management, and DocumentDB with MongoDB compatibility lets the application keep using MongoDB code, so there are no code changes and the least operational overhead.

x.A: Rekognition analyzes images and video. It doesn't do speaker recognition or transcription of calls.
x.B: Transcribe can transcribe calls and identify multiple speakers, and Athena can query the transcript files stored in S3, which can be retained for 7 years.
x.C: Translate converts text between languages and doesn't recognize speakers, and Redshift is costly for storing transcript files.
x.D: Rekognition isn't for speaker recognition, and Textract extracts text from documents and images, not for analyzing transcripts.

x.A: A Lambda authorizer works, but you have to write and maintain the validation code, which is more effort than using Cognito's built-in integration.
x.B: Creating API keys per user and validating them with Lambda is a lot of management, and API keys are not meant for user authentication.
x.C: Sending an email address in a header is insecure since anyone can fake it, and it also needs custom Lambda validation.
x.D: A Cognito user pool authorizer lets API Gateway validate the tokens that Cognito issued, with no custom code, and it is an AWS managed solution.
